storedTranscript.text: Hello, I'm Ryota, and welcome to your English lesson! Today we'll talk about your work and the projects you're involved in, and practice two grammar points: the present perfect and the past simple. Does that sound good?
I'm ready.

Great! First, I'd like to see what you can already do in English, so I know how to pitch today's lesson. This is a short, friendly chat, so don't worry about mistakes. Can you tell me a little about your job? What do you do?

Yes, I'm sales manager in the G I M R uh the GM uh general manager of that and I just supporting for the all division in the the company and of course most of the current of the management and the sales area for this.
Thanks, that's a clear picture of your role. Have you ever worked with an international customer? If so, can you tell me about the experience?
Yes, I have working with the international customer for sometimes.
That sounds like good experience. Which country is the customer from, and what do you usually do with them?

Uh, what I have the learn at the my company is uh connecting to the foreigner person because of a company has a lot of the foreigner and uh I have to using for my English to communicate for the each other.
Your company works with many people from other countries, so English is part of your daily work. Now, what is one skill you'd like to improve in your English, and why is it important to you?
Uh, I think in the future, I will supporting for the the global networking to the between the foreigner company and the Japanese company with my uh our directors.

Thank you. Global networking between your foreign partners and your Japanese directors is an important role. Today we'll work on making your grammar more accurate and your answers more natural. Let's start with your work. We use two tenses for experience. Look at the board.

Now, what are your main responsibilities at work? Please give me at least two sentences.

My main responsibility in sales area to the contact for the clients and supporting for the each division member about this and of course I have suggesting for the the new products about to the clients.

Good, you gave me two clear responsibilities. One small grammar point: you said "I have suggesting." With have, we use the past participle, so the verb is "suggested." Can you say that sentence again with the correct form?

I have suggested new products to my clients.

My main responsibility in the sales area is to be a contact for our clients, supporting for the each division member of of course the management for the each division member, and of course, uh suggesting for the new service and the project products to the clients.

Clear answer, thank you. One small thing: we say "supporting each division member", without "for". Now let's practise the present perfect.

Shall we go on, or do you have a question first?
and ready.

Let's go on. We use the present perfect for something that started in the past and is still true now.

Have you worked for your current company for a long time?
I have here over the 10 years.
Not quite. After "have," the sentence needs the past participle of the verb, and that's missing here. Try again, starting with: "I have worked here…"
I have working for our company for a long time. It takes about uh around the 10 years.

Close. The verb needs the past participle here: "have worked," not "have working." The sentence should be: I have worked for our company for about ten years.

That's the present perfect part done. Next is the past simple, for events at a specific time in the past. Shall we go on, or do you have a question first?
Yes.

Let's go on to the past simple. We use it for something finished at a specific time in the past, such as last year or two weeks ago.

Did you attend any business events or exhibitions last year? Tell me about one, in one or two sentences.
Yes, I attended the uh some business event in the uh Japan. last year.

Yes, "I attended" is the past simple, and "last year" tells us it's a finished time. One small thing: we say "in Japan," with no "the."

What was the event about, and what did you do there?
Uh, it's kind of the networking events, uh, the looking for the new uh business partner or the connecting for the the related our service.

Networking events are a good way to find new partners for your services. I'll put your idea into one sentence with the past simple.

This part is done. Next is a conversation about a project you're proud of. Shall we go on, or do you have a question first?
I'm ready.

Great, let's have a conversation about your work. I'll ask questions, and you can ask me some too.

What is one project you worked on that you're particularly proud of?
Uh, let me see is uh one project I worked in the supporting for the the the uh the uh SNS networking contents.

Thanks, you used the past simple there. One small thing: we say "I worked on a project" and "support the SNS content," without "for."

What was your role in that project?
Uh, my role is to manage for the member.
One small thing: we say "manage the members," without "for." Your role sounds like leadership in that project. What was the biggest challenge, and how did you handle it?
who is making for the content. uh, the talking about for the content. and making for the content.
Did you say you were in charge of the people who made the content? If so, we say "I managed the team that made the content." Is that what you meant?
I need to manage

Got it. You managed the team that made the content. A good sentence for that is:

 My role was to manage the team that created the SNS content.

What was the biggest challenge in that project?
Take your time. Was there a difficult part of that project? Just tell me one thing.
I'm not sure about it.
That's fine. Let's make it easier. Was it hard to communicate with the team, or was it hard to meet the deadline?
Uh, not project, but I have to find for the the new uh person to exchanging for the the uh the project members.

Thank you, so the challenge was finding a new person to exchange information with the project members. We say "exchange information with," with no "for."

That's this part done. Next, you can ask me a question about work, and then we can practise pronunciation if you like. Shall we go on, or do you have a question first?
Uh, because of is will leaving to our company and the project going on, so that's why I have to find a new people.

That makes sense: a team member is leaving, so you need a replacement. Say "a new person," not "new people," because you need one person.

Now it's your turn. Ask me a question about work, in English.
one more again.

Let's do one more, on the verb form that still gives you trouble.

Say the full sentence.
My responsibility in sales area is uh contact for our clients and supporting for the individual member and suggesting for the new product clients.

Thank you, that covers your role well. One small thing: we say "supporting the individual members," without "for."

The verb question is still on the board. Try it now and say the full sentence.

My responsibility in the sales area is to be the contact for our clients, to support each team member, and to suggest new products to clients.
Yes, for my our company above over the 10 years.
Did you mean "I have worked for our company for over ten years"? For the blank, give the past participle of "work" after "have." Can you say the full sentence once more?
I have worked with international customer

Yes, "I have worked" is the right form now. One small thing: we say "international customers," with an s, because you work with more than one customer.

That completes the verb practice. Next, you can ask me a question about work, and then we'll finish with a short summary. Shall we go on, or do you have a question first?
I have worked with international customer sometimes.

Almost. "Customer" needs an s here, because you work with more than one: I have worked with international customers sometimes. I have worked with international customers sometimes.

Do you have a question about work for me, or shall we go to the summary?
Yes, I have been working a project with uh uh us from another country, another uh countries.

That's a good project to be part of. One small thing: we say "working on a project," with "on."

Let's finish with a short summary.

You talked about your role, your team and a project you're proud of. One thing you did well was use the past simple clearly, for example "I attended a business event in Japan last year." To improve, keep the verb after "have" in the past participle, as in "I have worked for our company for about ten years."

Well done, and thank you for today's lesson. Keep practising these two grammar points when you talk about your work. Goodbye!
